stem.text: Some electrode potentials are given in Table 4.1.
Complete the equation that can be used to calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, ΔG⦵, for a cell reaction using the standard cell potential, E⦵cell.

explanation.text: ΔG⦵ = –nFE⦵cell, where n is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the cell reaction as written and F is the Faraday constant (96 500 C mol–1). The minus sign means that a positive cell potential gives a negative ΔG, so a reaction with a positive E⦵cell is feasible.

reasoningChain: Check the sign: positive E⦵cell must give negative ΔG⦵.

inferredMistakes.text: Leaving out the minus sign or n.

stem.text: An electrochemical cell is set up using a V<sup>3+</sup> / V<sup>2+</sup> electrode and a Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu electrode, both under standard conditions.
Write an equation for the cell reaction that occurs and calculate the value for E⦵cell.

explanation.text: The electrode with the more positive E<sup>⦵</sup> is where reduction happens. Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu (+0.34 V) is more positive than V<sup>3+</sup>/V<sup>2+</sup> (–0.26 V), so Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Cu and V<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised to V<sup>3+</sup>. Copper gains 2 electrons and each vanadium loses 1, so two V<sup>2+</sup> are needed for each Cu<sup>2+</sup>: Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2V<sup>2+</sup> → Cu + 2V<sup>3+</sup>.

E<sup>⦵</sup><sub>cell</sub> = E<sup>⦵</sup>(reduction) – E<sup>⦵</sup>(oxidation) = +0.34 – (–0.26) = +0.60 V. Electrode potentials are not multiplied when the half-equation is doubled. The MS ignores '0.6', so give 2 decimal places.

reasoningChain: Compare E⦵: Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34) is more positive than V³⁺/V²⁺ (–0.26), so Cu²⁺ is reduced.

inferredMistakes.text: Using the V²⁺/V electrode (–1.13 V) instead of the V³⁺/V²⁺ electrode named in the question.
Doubling the vanadium electrode potential when the half-equation is doubled.
Leaving electrons in the overall equation, which the MS treats as a contradiction.

stem.text: Identify two atoms or ions from Table 4.1 that will reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ under neutral conditions, but will not reduce Fe(OH)3 to Fe(OH)2 under alkaline conditions.

explanation.text: A species can reduce Fe<sup>3+</sup> to Fe<sup>2+</sup> if its own electrode potential (as the reduced form) is less positive than +0.77 V, because then E<sup>⦵</sup><sub>cell</sub> is positive. To fail to reduce Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub>, its electrode potential must be more positive than –0.56 V. So the reducing agent must come from a couple with E<sup>⦵</sup> between –0.56 V and +0.77 V.

Two couples fit: Cu2+/Cu (+0.34 V), where the reducing agent is Cu, and V3+/V2+ (–0.26 V), where the reducing agent is V2+. V (–1.13 V) is too strong because it would also reduce Fe(OH)3, and Cl– (+1.36 V) is too weak to reduce Fe3+.

reasoningChain: The reducing agent is the right-hand species of a couple.
It must reduce Fe³⁺: its E⦵ must be below +0.77 V.
It must not reduce Fe(OH)₃: its E⦵ must be above –0.56 V.
Couples between –0.56 and +0.77 V: Cu²⁺/Cu and V³⁺/V²⁺, so the answers are Cu and V²⁺.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving the oxidised forms (Cu²⁺, V³⁺) instead of the species that actually act as reducing agents.
Including V, which is a strong enough reductant to reduce Fe(OH)₃ as well.

stem.text: Identify the strongest oxidising agent and the strongest reducing agent in Table 4.1.

guidance: CON if both oxidised and reduced form given.
CON if both oxidised and reduced form given.

explanation.text: Oxidising agents are on the left of the half-equations (they gain electrons). The most positive E⦵ (+1.36 V) belongs to Cl2/Cl–, so Cl2 is the strongest oxidising agent. Reducing agents are on the right (they lose electrons). The most negative E⦵ (–1.13 V) belongs to V2+/V, so V is the strongest reducing agent.

reasoningChain: Most positive E⦵: Cl₂/Cl⁻ → left-hand species Cl₂ is the strongest oxidising agent.
Most negative E⦵: V²⁺/V → right-hand species V is the strongest reducing agent.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving Cl⁻ or V²⁺, the species on the wrong side of the half-equation.
Naming both forms of a couple (e.g. 'Cl₂/Cl⁻'), which the MS treats as a contradiction.

stem.text:
A dilute solution of NaOH(aq) is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
A steady current of 2.40 A is passed for 2.00 hours.
Calculate the mass, in g, of oxygen that is released at the anode.

explanation.text: The MS gives no answer for this part: every candidate was awarded all three marks, so the published scheme does not show the expected working. The steps below are the standard method, not the official MS.

At the anode, hydroxide ions are oxidised: 4OH<sup>–</sup> → O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e<sup>–</sup>. The charge passed is Q = It = 2.40 × 2.00 × 3600 = 17 280 C. Moles of electrons = 17 280 / 96 500 = 0.179 mol. Four electrons release one O<sub>2</sub>, so moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 0.179 / 4 = 0.0448 mol, and the mass is 0.0448 × 32.0 = 1.43 g.

inferredMistakes.text: Using 2.00 as the time in seconds or minutes instead of converting 2.00 hours to 7200 s.
Dividing by 2 instead of 4 (treating O₂ like H₂), or using the mass of O atoms (16) instead of O₂ (32).
